title: Investigating the origins of partisanship: What motivates children to preferentially endorse their ingroups' claims?
abstract: People tend to endorse empirical claims along partisan lines, sometimes agreeing with their ingroup even when the evidence suggests otherwise. A developmental approach can clarify the motives underlying this phenomenon by revealing which are fundamental to its emergence. We tested two plausible motives: Do children preferentially endorse their ingroup's empirical claims because they treat the ingroup as a reliable guide to truth (an epistemic motive), or because endorsing these claims affirms their relationship to the group (an affiliative motive)? Study 1 (N = 98; ages 5-7) established the basic phenomenon: Children assigned to a minimal group endorsed their ingroup's claims more often than children in a yoked no-group control condition, confirming that group membership provides a partisan boost beyond what perceptual evidence alone would warrant. Studies 2 and 3 then probed motives in complementary ways: In Study 2 (N = 208; ages 6-9), we allowed children to respond privately, removing the public context in which endorsement most effectively serves to affirm their relationship to the group. In Study 3 (N = 172; ages 6-9), we incentivized accuracy, heightening children's sensitivity to the evidence. Partisan endorsement was absent under private responding and under accuracy incentives. Because genuine epistemic trust should persist in private and under incentives for truth, this overall pattern was more consistent with an affiliative motive than an epistemic one: Children's partisan endorsement appears to serve a group-relational function rather than a truth-seeking one. These findings speak to the motivational and developmental origins of partisan cognition.
